paragraphs.heading: What a monsoon is
paragraphs.text: A monsoon was traditionally a wind that reverses with the seasons, bringing a matching change in rainfall. Today the word also covers seasonal shifts in air circulation and rain tied to the yearly swing of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), which moves back and forth between limits north and south of the equator. In everyday use, monsoon usually means the rainy phase, though there is also a dry phase. It can even mean short bursts of heavy local rain.

paragraphs.heading: What drives it
paragraphs.text: Monsoons were once explained as a giant sea breeze, caused by land getting hotter than the ocean. That idea is no longer accepted. The monsoon is now seen as a planetary-scale pattern involving the ITCZ's yearly migration between its northern and southern limits. How far the ITCZ reaches depends on the heating contrast between land and sea, and in South Asia the high Tibetan Plateau is thought to influence how far north the monsoon goes.

paragraphs.heading: Where and the word
paragraphs.text: The world's major monsoon systems are found in West Africa, across South Asia and Australia, and in both North and South America. The word entered English in British India and nearby countries, where it named the big seasonal southwest winds off the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea that brought heavy rain. Its origin is not fully certain. English took it from Portuguese monção, which goes back to the Arabic mawsim, meaning season, partly by way of early modern Dutch.

paragraphs.heading: Deep origins
paragraphs.text: The strengthening of the Asian monsoon has been tied to the rise of the Tibetan Plateau after the Indian subcontinent collided with Asia around 50 million years ago. Records from the Arabian Sea and wind-blown dust in China's Loess Plateau led many geologists to think the monsoon first became strong about 8 million years ago. More recent evidence from plant fossils in China and long sediment records from the South China Sea points instead to a start 15–20 million years ago, linked to early uplift of Tibet. Testing this idea awaits deep ocean drilling.

paragraphs.heading: Ice ages and the sea
paragraphs.text: Since then the monsoon's strength has changed a great deal, largely in step with global climate change, especially the Pleistocene ice ages. Marine plankton suggest the South Asian Monsoon grew stronger around 5 million years ago. During ice periods sea level fell, the Indonesian Seaway closed, and cold Pacific water was held back from the Indian Ocean; the warmer Indian Ocean that resulted is believed to have intensified the monsoons. A 2018 study found monsoon rainfall in South Asia was much lower during glacial periods than in interglacial periods like today.

paragraphs.heading: The East Asian record
paragraphs.text: The East Asian Summer Monsoon has its own long record. It was weaker in the cold spells of glacial periods such as the Last Glacial Maximum and stronger in warmer times. It reached a high point around 6,000 years ago, in the Middle Holocene. Then it began to fade around 5,000 to 4,500 years ago and has kept weakening to the present day.
